# Repository instructions

This project is a fork from typescript-language-features extension of VSCode, the source code can be accessed from directory /Users/chemzqm/lib/vscode/extensions/typescript-language-features

## Scope

These instructions apply to the whole repository unless a more specific AGENTS.md exists below it.

This repository produces a coc.nvim extension for Vim and Neovim. VS Code or another editor extension may be an upstream source, but it is not the runtime target. Preserve a reliable Coc user experience before pursuing textual similarity with upstream.

For repositories with no editor-extension upstream, apply the general development and validation rules and ignore the upstream-specific sections.

## Priorities

1. Keep the extension correct on supported coc.nvim, Vim, Neovim, and Node.js versions.
2. Preserve documented or tested Coc-only behavior and public identifiers.
3. Port relevant upstream fixes and features without importing VS Code runtime assumptions.
4. Minimize unnecessary divergence where doing so does not weaken the first three priorities.
5. Follow this repository’s existing architecture, scripts, formatting, and release conventions.

## Start every task

• Read git status --short and preserve unrelated user changes.
• Read package.json, the active lockfile, build configuration, relevant documentation, nearby tests, and scoped instruction files before editing.
• Use the package manager selected by the checked-in lockfile. Use existing scripts rather than inventing parallel commands.
• Inspect the installed coc.nvim dependency’s types and implementation before assuming an API exists or matches VS Code.
• Keep the change within the requested scope. Do not update unrelated dependencies, generated files, documentation, or formatting.

## Ownership boundaries

Classify each touched area before changing it:

• Upstream-derived core: editor-neutral logic, protocols, language-server code, parsers, and utilities that should usually track upstream.
• Coc adaptation boundary: activation, API translation, commands, configuration access, UI integration, events, URI/filetype handling, and lifecycle wiring.
• Coc-owned behavior: features, fixes, defaults, commands, compatibility choices, or UX created specifically for Vim/Neovim and Coc users.
• Generated or vendored content: files that must be changed through their generator or documented update procedure.

If ownership is unclear, treat the code as Coc adaptation or Coc-owned until history, tests, or documentation prove otherwise.

## Synchronizing an upstream VS Code extension

Use the $coc-vscode-sync skill before editing. Do not begin the port until the exact upstream source and old-to-new revision range, Coc protected surfaces, and a per-change decision table are known.

• Synchronize behavior, bug fixes, protocol changes, and safe shared logic; do not synchronize files merely because paths or names match.
• Classify every upstream change as adopt, adapt, or skip, with a short reason and planned validation.
• Apply small semantic patches. Never replace Coc files or package.json wholesale with their upstream versions.
• Preserve Coc adapters around shared code. A cleaner upstream abstraction is not sufficient reason to remove a Coc-specific path.
• Re-check Coc-only commits and current behavior with git log, git blame, tests, documentation, and manifest entries. Import markers alone are not proof of ownership.
• Keep deliberate divergences explicit. Do not disguise unsupported VS Code functionality as parity.

## Coc behavior that must not regress

• Extension activation/deactivation, subscriptions, cancellation, disposal, restart, and shutdown behavior.
• Imports and integrations through coc.nvim, including providers, language clients, workspace events, commands, configuration, output, status, lists, quickfix, prompts, and notifications.
• Published command IDs, configuration keys, defaults, scopes, activation events, language IDs, filetypes, URI schemes, and user-visible behavior unless the task explicitly changes them.
• Vim/Neovim-specific workflows, including headless operation and environments without a DOM, Electron, VS Code workbench services, or VS Code storage/authentication APIs.
• Language-server discovery, download, verification, launch arguments, transports, environment, workspace selection, logging, recovery, and platform-specific paths.

Do not add a runtime dependency on vscode. Do not copy VS Code telemetry, experiments, authentication, marketplace, task, webview, status-bar, or workbench code unless the task explicitly requires a supported Coc equivalent.

## API adaptation

• Verify semantics, not just names, when mapping VS Code APIs to coc.nvim APIs.
• Prefer a small explicit adapter when shared upstream logic is valuable. Do not build a broad VS Code compatibility layer speculatively.
• Preserve ordering, cancellation, error propagation, resource ownership, and disposal when translating asynchronous APIs.
• Use Coc-native UI and lifecycle primitives. Skip an upstream feature when no reliable Coc equivalent exists and the request does not require designing one.
• Preserve documented Coc public behavior. Do not add legacy shims solely to mimic obsolete upstream behavior.

## Manifests, dependencies, and generated files

• Merge only relevant manifest contributions. Preserve Coc engine constraints, activation behavior, command/configuration IDs, scripts, packaging, and publish metadata.
• Inspect a dependency’s installed source, documentation, and types before adding code around a capability it may already provide.
• Add or update a dependency only when required by the port. Explain lockfile changes and avoid unrelated version churn.
• Rebuild generated files with the repository’s generator. Never hand-edit bundled output unless the repository explicitly treats it as source.
• Check licensing and packaging before copying upstream source, schemas, assets, binaries, or language-server artifacts.

## Testing

For an upstream port, test both the upstream behavior and the Coc boundary it crosses.

1. Run type checking or compilation with the repository’s existing script.
2. Run tests use coc-test

## Change discipline

• Make the smallest coherent diff that fully implements the requested behavior.
• Preserve public IDs and defaults unless changing them is an explicit, tested decision.
• Update comments and documentation that would otherwise become false; do not rewrite unrelated prose.
• Do not commit, push, publish, force-update branches, or rewrite history unless the user explicitly requests it.
• Never discard unrelated work to make an upstream patch apply.

## Documentation

• Update `history.md` whenever a change is merged or synced: record user-visible
  changes (new/removed/changed commands, configurations, behaviors, fixes) under
  the current version section, matching the existing style. Never leave a merged
  or synced change unrecorded.
• For upstream syncs, also update `migrate.md`: list the ported upstream commits
  and the upstream changes intentionally not ported, with reasons.
• When the user asks to "整理提交" (organize commits), keep code changes and
  documentation updates (including `history.md`/`migrate.md`) as separate,
  reviewable commits.
